insights.topic: Verified purchase intent vs. probabilistic targeting
insights.insight: Crinkl's protocol has crossed $5M cumulative verified GMV across 104,000+ receipts — each one a cryptographically confirmed transaction, not an inferred intent signal. For brands paying $5+ CPM on probabilistic audience data, this represents a structurally different input: deterministic proof of purchase at the category and store level.

Over the trailing 14 days, grocery-supermarkets led with 1,179 receipts ($52,889), followed by retail-department-stores at 705 receipts ($28,742) and restaurants-dining at 859 receipts ($26,315) — a distribution that maps directly to the categories where brand marketers most need closed-loop purchase verification.

The top five brands by 14-day receipt count are Walmart (299), Kroger (132), Target (129), Publix (129), and Costco (106) — a list dominated by mass and grocery channels where national CPG brands compete hardest for verified shelf-level data.

insights.topic: Publix entry signals Southeast geographic expansion
insights.insight: Publix's first appearance on the thresholded brand list — tying Target at 129 receipts — is notable because Publix's footprint is concentrated in the Southeast US; its emergence suggests either new coverage in that region or meaningfully deeper penetration of an existing user base there, making it a leading indicator of geographic reach for brands with Southeast exposure.

The New York–Newark–Jersey City metro appeared in the protocol's active coverage cells for the first time in the current observation window; given its scale, this is the single most consequential geographic addition logged to date and expands the addressable verified-receipt universe for any brand with Northeast retail or foodservice presence.

insights.topic: Throughput trend: trough floors rising, ceiling uncertain
insights.insight: Post-rolloff GMV troughs have risen three consecutive cycles ($60,852 → $64,666 → $67,412), and the most recent pre-rolloff peak at $77,466 broke a three-cycle compression sequence — suggesting the protocol's sustainable weekly throughput is drifting upward even if it has not reclaimed the prior $83.5K plateau; for brands evaluating data volume adequacy, the floor trend is the more reliable planning input than peak readings.
